CB panel debate - SEX EDUCATION [6110]

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's parents versus teachers... should the government determine who teaches young school children about sex?

Unique Selling Point:
Four experts around one table, go toe-to-toe in Carte Blanche's second panel debate for 2022. Under harsh studio lights, we turn the heat up on a topic that some say shouldn't be up for debate, but rather, ready to be implemented.

Summary:
They're taking away our rights to decide for our own children.... well, that's at least what some irate parents are saying as government pushes forward with its plans to bring the big "birds and the bees" talk, right into the classroom.

But its not just about WHO teaches your child about their bodies and sex, it's also about WHEN your child is ready for sex education... should nine year olds really be exposed to conversations about sex or are parents failing them by shying away from these difficult conversations in their own homes?

Further information:
In 2019, a leaked report from the Department of Basic Education, demonstrated how government was moving forward with its plans to make sex education a priority in the classroom. The contents includes lessons on "what 'private parts' are and the biological names for them" for Grade 4 learners, masturbation for Grade 7 learners and "a seven-step, illustrated depiction of how a female condom should be correctly placed" for Grade 9 learners.

Additionally, the document showed that learners in grade 10 and 11 would be learning about "various sexual orientations" and transgender people.

The South African Teachers Union called it "grossly insensitive", some parents said it was inappropriate for their children while government insisted that educating learners on "issues of Gender-Based Violence" is a central concern for the Department of Basic Education.

In a country with record high numbers of statutory rape and teen pregnancies, is sex education from nine years old, really the answer?

Director of Child Law Adv Karabo Ozah says there's no question - educating and empowering children about sex is the answer.

But Freedom of Religion SA and the SA Teachers Union beg to differ - they say, sex doesn't belong in the classroom.

Four experts, one big debate...

Press Release:


Carte Blanche Debates: Comprehensive Sexuality Education

As government pushes ahead with its plans to bring comprehensive sexuality education into the classroom, some irate parents are saying the content is “grossly inappropriate” for their young children. Four experts go toe-to-toe in this second instalment of Carte Blanche Debates as we ask: should young children be exposed to conversations about sex at school, or should that part of their education be left to parents?

Producer: Chwayitisa Futshane | Research: Ayanda Charlie |

Moderator: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje

Script:


Teen pregnancies, risky sexual behavior, and a lack of knowledge about HIV prevention: a recipe for a crisis in our schools.

The Department of Education says it’s concerned that children are becoming exposed to sexual activity at a far younger age --- forcing a re-think on sex education in schools.

But there’s pushback, with some parents arguing the content is “grossly inappropriate” for younger children.

So, is it government’s place to teach children about sex and sexuality in the classroom?

Or should it be left to parents?

I’m Busisiwe Gumede-Chi---zhan---je…

Stating their cases tonight: Levi Singh – a youth development advocate for SAT Regional and Afriyan ….


Research and advocacy officer for section 27 – Julia Chaskalson


Attorney and activist Pearl Kupe


and CEO of the Suid-Afrikaanse Onderwysers Unie Chris Klopper…

Let’s debate…

Busisiwe: Please set us up, tell us a bit more about what comprehensive sexuality education is and is it different from what we’ve had in the past?

LEVI: it needs to be medically appropriate and it needs to have an emphasis on human rights and gender equality and this sort of education needs to be culturally relevant, and contextual to a country’s context.

09:00 - we believe that comprehensive sexuality education if done right, can put an adolescent young person, onto a happy, healthy safe pathway to adulthood and that’s our approach to CSE.

BUSISIWE: And Julia what would that look like in the classroom?

09:17 - JULIA: … It’s about sexual and reproductive health, how to prevent a pregnancy, giving learners information about the changes that their bodies might be going through… in addition to these kind of important public health conversations, it’s also about addressing different attitudes and behaviors.

09:47 – So we often talk about in South Africa, the gender-based violence pandemic but in terms of actually shifting the attitudes that drive that pandemic, the attitudes of patriarchy or the attitudes of violence, CSE is a really critical tool for shaping that.

10:04 – So really this is about answering learners questions that they might have about their own bodies, their development, their identities, their.


BUSISIWE – Sure… Chris it sounds like a solid subject that will empower our children to make sound decisions about their lives, why are you against?

CHRIS: … we also believe that CSE is a necessary tool, a necessary subject. Our problem is with regards to the detail and the how of it and more specifically the scripted lesson plans and the fact that the assessment of learners will be based on the lesson plan. …. it is not community specific, it is not religious specific and what we would like to see is less of a one-size fits all approach but an approach that would be appropriate to a particular community and where a particular community would have a say in what is taught and how it is taught and by whom it is taught.

11:32 – PEARL - 12:11 - …we don’t have a problem with the fact that children need to know about their sexuality, it’s the how. How is it done? Is it appropriate for them and who is involved. You can’t exclude parents from this. To not consult and to exclude the family from that process, I think is highly dangerous. So it’s also the detail. The how and the who are in volved.

12:42 – There was a serious lack of consultation here and I think it needs to be addressed. …parents are the ones who know their children. They’re the ones and you can’t have a one size fits all.
You cannot have a situation where the state is taking over the parenting function.

13:52 – JULIA: I don’t disagree that parents are an incredibility important role player in this conversation, but in a context where a lot of these learners struggle to have these sensitive discussions with older care givers or parents, in a context where many learners actually don’t have parents who are active in their lives, the classroom is an important space to kind of fill in the gaps. … I think a lot of learners struggle to have these conversations with you know, if it’s about their identity, their sexuality, it may be challenging to have these conversations with a parent


17:59 – PEARL: We’ve actually developed an alternative called family sexuality education which is first prize because it includes the parents in terms of developing a wholistic and comprehensive approach.. not just teaching children about their sexual reproduction, but in terms of their identity, in terms of being able to stand against bullying.

18:57 – LEVI: To Pearl’s point, there should be some consideration around the scripted lesson plans and their current content viz a viz, the amount of disinformation and misinfornmation that has been spread online and on social media in particular with regards to the content. If anyone reads through the current scripted lesson plans in their current state, there are specific lessons that talk to substance abuse, to anti-bullying, to gender based violence. Over 26 percent of the content in the scripted lesson plans, speaks specifically to issues relating to violence.

.

2020 JULIA –

20:50 – When it comes to the scripted lesson plans, I think there has been a kind of uproar and outrage about them and sometimes facts have been selected quite specifically and I think blown out of proportion.
I think parents are really important kind of actor in this too but in a context where a lot of parents don’t want to have these conversations and are trying to avoid it and trying to shut it down. That silence is a breeding ground for violence, for sexual health risks, for mental health risks too.

21:46 – BUSISIWE: I don’t remember having the talk with my parents do you Chris…

21:49 – CHRIS: I had a brief talk with my father once and he asked me, do I know what’s going on in life and I said, Thank I know. {laughter} I said please go on with it…[laughter}


BUSISIWE: Does CSE encourage children to explore their sexuality?

26:20 – JULIA – I think again this is something that has been blown out of proportion. The focus that it will encourage promiscuity or encourage a type of sexuality that is perceived as foreign, I think is unfair to learners in the classroom, including lgbt learners who have to questions about their bodies, questions about their rights, questions about their identities that need to be answered… there’s nothing in these slps, that says this is how you have sex, and this… there’s nothing that encourages that. What it does is that it acknowledges that learners are going to experiment, learners are curious, learners are interacting with their peers, and sometimes in the SA context, a lot of young girls are interacting with older men and it equips them with information about how they can make healthy and informed decisions within this context.

27:29 – CHRIS: … let’s look at this from an educational perspective. In all the other subjects, teachers have a choice with regards to teaching and learning material. In all the subjects, except in this particular one. Here is a mandatory, scripted lesson plan, that’s the problem.

Our problem lies with the scripted lesson plans, where we say, give a choice to a community with regards to what and how it is taught.

JULIA – ... The idea behind the SLPs was cognizant that teachers have a lot of work on their plate, they might not, if they are not trained, have the time, to develop lesson material about these really important subjects… To think of these SLPs as this imposition that you have to read it word for word, limits the agency of teachers, when this is supposed to be a resource that assists them to have conversations that many of them want to have but don’t feel equipped to do so. …. that these lesson plans should be seen as a set of guidelines about what is age appropriate in terms of learner development, in terms of what is scientifically accurate and what learners need to know at each stage through their transition through adolescents as opposed to this doctrine that needs to be read word for word. It could be a very valuable resource.

29:55 – CHRIS: But it’s not completely true, the assessment of LO and CSE will be based on the scripted lesson plans. That’s the problem. There is not a question of it being a guideline, it’s a mandatory lesson plan that has to be followed. And that’s a problem.

This is where the rights of teachers also come. What about a teacher who feels offended by it? That teaher has a right.


34:23 BUSISIWE: And what do the numbers tell us about children having sex with other children? And exploring with other kids as well? That age seems to be getting younger and younger?

34:35 LEVI: So the age of sexual debut in the SA context is also quite low. On average researchers have put it between the ages 10 – 14 which is far below the global average which is around 16-18. And that also talks to the issue of coerced sex among adolescents – younger adolscents and older adolescents and again it points to the failure of delivering timely, age and developmentally appropriate information for adolescents to navigate this transition into adulthood.


Well thank you all for your thoughts on this controversial issue.
Clearly, there are no easy answers. Parents and government both have roles to play in shaping our children’s education. And, few would disagree, that at its center is ensuring our children’s rights are protected.
